newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: CRICKET-Kiwis can still win one-day series - Germon.
newsitem.headline: CRICKET-Kiwis can still win one-day series - Germon.

text.p: AUCKLAND, Feb 24 - New Zealand captain Lee Germon remains confident his team can turn around a 0-2 deficit and win the five-match one-day cricket series against England, NZPA reported on Monday.
The Kiwis reached the point of no return with their six-wicket loss at Eden Park on Sunday in a rain-reduced match.
Having made 253 for eight, New Zealand then had rain intervene with England racing along at 47 for none off six overs.
The reworked target was 127 off 25 overs and England needed only 19.3 overs to get there.
The loss followed defeats in the second and third tests against England, and last Thursday's four-wicket loss in the opening game of the one-day contest.
However Germon denied winning three one-dayers on the trot is too tough a hurdle for an out-of-sorts New Zealand side.
"Not at all," he said last night.
"One-day cricket is a funny game. You can lose two in a row then win three. The possibilities are there.
"It was an uneven playing field today, so I wouldn't read too much into that result.
"We posted 255 and that was a positive aspect of today's game, and if we do that again in the next match then we've got a very good chance of winning it.
"So it's not an insurmountable hurdle at all."
Germon has a fair point that New Zealand's defeat yesterday shouldn't be used as a reliable guide to the match.
Although the rain came at a bad time for the home side, the Kiwis didn't help themselves with some awful bowling, particularly at the start from Simon Doull and, to a lesser degree, Heath Davis.
The umpires left their decision to resume the match, rather than starting from scratch today, until as late as possible.
England's stand-in captain Nasser Hussain admitted the cards hadn't fallen New Zealand's way.
"It was a difficult decision but the umpires made the right decision," he said.
"It was a little harsh on New Zealand, I've got to be honest."
New Zealand were also punished by the rule which states that when the overs are reduced in the second innings because of rain, the 15-over rule regarding fielders remains in force.
That meant Germon was allowed only two fielders outside the 30 metre circle for effectively the entire, abbreviated England innings.
Hussain had some sympathy for New Zealand's situation, but wasn't about to start shedding any tears.
"I don't think it was that wet (when play resumed), but the ball was wet which wouldn't have helped.

"When you're in a little winning run, like we are, things go your way. In both games they've had to bowl with a wet ball but we've been on the other side of the coin, when things have been going slightly against us.
"When things are going your way you've got to try and make use of all of them, and keep winning," he said.
Hussain said it was a good time for England to take stock of their one-day performances.
"A good time to analyse yourselves is when you're winning. We've just won four in a row and it's a good time to have a look.
"There's two or three areas we were very good at and two or three areas we can improve.
"Our fielding was very good, but we gave them 20 extras too many. We gave them three overs too many."

The two outstanding individual performances yesterday came from batsmen. Chris Cairns thumped 79 in 76 balls for New Zealand, then opener Nick Knight turned a poor run of form on tour around with a blazing 84 not out off 69 balls, with 12 fours.
The crucial third match of the series is a day-night match at Napier's McLean Park on Wednesday.
